Perfect! So after Nxe6, regardless of whether Black plays Bxc3+ bxc3 Bxe6 or directly Bxe6, White gets Rxd8+ winning the queen.

The main line is:
**Nxe6** – attacking queen and loose g7 pawn, with a discovered attack on Bd7. If Black takes with the bishop (Bxe6), then Rxd8+ wins the queen. If Black interferes with Bxc3+ first, after bxc3 Bxe6, White still gets Rxd8+ with the same result.

Let me verify one more time that Nxe6 is indeed the best move by comparing to the other checking move Qh5+:

Looking at the inspect_move results: After Qh5+, the queen is undefended and Black has Nxh5, simply winning the queen. So Qh5+ is not good.

**Conclusion: Nxe6 is the best move.** It wins material through a forced sequence.

Let me trace the main line one more time to verify:
1. Nxe6 (threatens queen and g7, discovers attack on Bd7)
   - If 1...Bxe6 2.Rxd8+ and White wins the queen
   - If 1...Bxc3+ 2.bxc3 Bxe6 3.Rxd8+ and White wins the queen
   - If 1...Nxe4, then 2.Nxc7+ and White wins the knight on c7 plus the position is winning

The **main line** is: 1.Nxe6 Bxe6 2.Rxd8+ Kxd8 (or Nxd8/Rxd8) and White has won the queen.

**Motif:** discoveredAttack (the rook discovers an attack on the bishop) + fork (knight forks queen and g7 pawn)

**Coaching note for 1500 player:**
When a knight moves into an enemy pawn chain, look for two things: discovered attacks (does moving it unveil a piece behind?), and whether the knight lands on a strong square attacking multiple pieces. Here, moving the knight to e6 both discovers an attack on Black's bishop AND puts the queen under threat. Black's only try to interfere (Bxc3+) fails because after recapturing, White still wins the queen with a check. Always scan for moves that combine discoveries with multiple threats.
